figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. Chemical structures of four typical NRLPs, including daptomycin, polymyxin E, surfactin, and fengycin C. The fatty acid chains of these
NRLP drugs are highlighted in red. Among them, daptomycin exhibits activity against Gram-positive bacteria, polymyxin E targets Gram-negative
bacteria, and surfactin and fengycin C, in addition to their surfactant properties, also demonstrate antimicrobial activity.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Concept of the “Starter Unit” and combinatorial biosynthesis of the starter unit. (a) The “Starter Unit” concept for NRLPs involves the
lipoinitiation pathway and initiation module, where the lipoinitiation pathway is also associated with primary metabolism and the supply of
precursors/substrates. (b) Combinatorial biosynthesis of the starter unit focuses on several key strategies, including enhancing precursor and
substrate availability, modifying lipoinitiation pathways, and engineering the initiation module.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption: Figure 3. Obtaining high-purity daptomycin products and reducing byproduct formation through feeding precursor/substrates.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Genetic engineering of the starter unit of the cda
biosynthetic gene cluster to obtain novel derivatives. (a) The starter
unit of CDA primarily involves the lipoinitiation pathway, which
includes enzymes such as FabF3, FabH4, FAS, ACP, HxcO, and
HcmO, and the lipoinitiation module, which encompasses the
CdaPS1-Cs domain. Following this, other modules in the core
assembly line, from CdaPS1 to CdaPS3, work in concert to assemble
the final product, CDA4a. (b) Combinatorial biosynthesis of the
starter unit of CDA by FabF3 mutations and substrate analog feeding.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Combinatorial biosynthesis of the starter unit in the dpt gene cluster facilitates the production of high-purity daptomycin without
substrate feeding. This primarily involves the introduction of the T1 FAS pathway and TE enzymes to increase the fatty acid pool and the selection
of more selective/active FAAL enzymes for the efficient activation of decanoic acid.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 6. Canonical structure of the Cs domain illustrated using
CDA-Cs as an example (PDB: 4JN3). The “latch” and “floor” regions
in the N-lobe are thought to be crucial in mediating interactions and
may also be responsive to conformational changes. Additionally, the
conserved HHxxxDG motif in the condensation domains is widely
recognized as the active center, playing a key role in catalysis.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 7. Crystal structure of the Cs domain bound to an acyl-CoA substrate and the reaction cycle for the Cs domain. (a) The crystal structure of
the Cs domain (RzmA-Cs R148A mutant with C8-CoA, PDB: 7C1L) reveals key residues within the binding pocket, including Q36, Q136, Y138,
R148, and M143, which are critical for determining the Cs domain’s specificity for fatty acyl-CoA substrates. These residues are believed to play a
pivotal role in substrate recognition. (b) Proposed substrate condensation cycle of the Cs domain based on structural data (PDB: 7C1P, 7C1S, and
7C1U). The relative movement between the latch and floor regions determines the conformational changes in the protein. Briefly, after substrate
binding, residues within the “latch” and “floor” regions reposition their side chains toward the active site, causing the substrate tunnel to constrict
(bound state). Following the condensation reaction, the Cs domain partially opens, accompanied by a significant upward movement of the “floor”
loop, which pushes CoA out of the “donor” site (released state). Finally, the two lobes fully open, and the “floor” loop shifts downward (inbound
state), initiating a new catalytic cycle.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 8
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 8. Engineering of the Cs domain to modify its specificities for fatty acid substrates. (a) Point mutations in the Cs domain to enlarge the
binding pocket, enabling the accommodation of longer acyl-CoA substrates and generating extended lipo-chain derivatives. Key mutations at
positions Q136, Y138, M143, and R148 alter the substrate specificity, with R148 at the pocket entrance being critical for determining the fatty acid
chain length. The other residues, positioned deeper in the pocket, influence the overall substrate recognition. Combinatorial mutations further
expand the binding pocket, enabling the incorporation of longer acyl chains and the generation of novel lipopeptide derivatives. (b) Domain and
subdomain swapping of the Cs domain to alter the lipid chains in NRLPs.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 9
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 9. High-throughput screening of Cs domain mutants using the yeast surface display technology. To simulate in vitro reaction conditions, the
CAT module, derived from surfactin synthetase SrfA-C, was displayed on the yeast surface and used in conjunction with a downstream free ATE
module (derived from the first module, TycA, of tyrocidine synthetase A) for assembly line reactions. The communication between the upstream
and downstream modules was facilitated through docking domains. After successfully condensing the substrates with a terminal alkyne on the
downstream substrate, the alkyne-containing product was fluorescently labeled using a click reaction. This enabled high-throughput fluorescence
screening to identify mutants with high reactivity. Subsequently, the upstream TycA module was optimized by replacing its A domain with maltose-
binding protein to improve protein solubility and allow fatty acid to load onto the T domain. Combined with the SrfA-C-Cs-A-T-TE module, this
engineered module enabled efficient high-throughput screening of Cs domain mutants, identifying mutants with high specificity for particular fatty
acid substrates.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 10
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 10. Catalytic mechanism of FAAL and its fatty acid−binding pocket. (a) The catalytic mechanism of FAAL involves two key steps: 1)
adenylation reaction: the fatty acid substrate is activated through the hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), forming an acyl-AMP
intermediate. 2) Thiolation reaction: the acyl-AMP intermediate is transferred to the thiol group on the Ppant arm of the ACP or PCP domain
within the NRPS. Finally, the fatty acyl-ACP or -PCP is incorporated into the NRLPs by the C domain within the NRPS assembly line. (b) The
crystal structure of FAAL bound to AMP-C18:1 (PDB number: 8I6M), showing the monomeric structure of the enzyme.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 11
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 11. Complete reaction cycle of FAAL. From step 1 to step 8, the reaction cycle begins with fatty acids entering the reaction tunnel, followed
by binding of ATP to a pocket adjacent to the tunnel. AMP is then transferred to the carboxyl group of the fatty acid, forming an acyl-AMP
intermediate. Upon formation of this intermediate, ACP-Ppant enters through the opening of the N-terminal domain of FAAL. Subsequently,
FAAL undergoes a conformational change, transitioning to a closed state. The acyl group is transferred to the Ppant of ACP, generating fatty acyl-
ACP and releasing AMP. After the product is released, FAAL returns to its open conformation. (Related crystallization structures: 8I35, 8I3I, 8I49,
8I51, 8I6M, 8I8D, and 8I8E).
